surfeit

SUR-fit · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Surfeit is an excessive amount of something.

A surfeit of last-minute donations meant the shelter had far more supplies than it could use.

Example

The harvest produced such a surfeit of zucchini that neighbors began leaving bags of it on each other's porches.

This wasn't just a good harvest -- it was so much more than anyone actually needed that it became almost a burden, which is exactly a surfeit.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

excess: An excess is any amount beyond what is needed — even one extra chair makes an excess. A surfeit is a heavier word: so much of something, often food or pleasures, that the abundance itself turns wearying or unwelcome.

glut: A glut is an oversupply in a market — a glut of oil or of unsold cars drives prices down. A surfeit belongs to people and appetites: more food, praise, or entertainment than anyone can happily take in.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

scarcity: a lack or shortage of something

Where it sits · how far past enough it goes — bounty → surfeit → overload

bounty vs. surfeit: A bounty is a generous, welcome amount; a surfeit is so much that it becomes excessive or even unwelcome.

overload vs. surfeit: A surfeit describes an excessive supply of something; an overload implies that excess has become genuinely overwhelming or unmanageable.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — sur-

prefix — sur-: over, above (Latin (super-))

root — feit

root — feit: to do, make (Latin (facere))

Put it together

Put it together: Surfeit comes from Old French surfaire, from Latin super- ('over') + facere ('to do, make') -- literally 'to overdo,' describing something made or done to excess.

Use the root in a new word: factory

Use the root in a new word: factory: The factory across town makes thousands of bicycle parts every single day.

Word Building

Word Choice

Surfeit is a noun, almost always used with "of" (a surfeit of food, a surfeit of applicants), describing an amount so large it becomes burdensome rather than simply generous.
